hints: Notice the $3.2 \text{ mA}$ conventional current through R from X to Y along the bottom wire, and recall that electron flow is opposite to conventional current.
Recall that current is rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$, and each electron carries charge of magnitude $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Convert $3.2 \text{ mA}$ to $3.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}$ and divide by $e$ to get the number of electrons per second, checking that the power of 10 is large and positive.
walkthrough: Identify the conventional current direction through R. Outside the cell current flows from positive to negative, giving a conventional current from X to Y through the bottom resistor.
State the electron direction rule. Electrons are negatively charged so their drift is opposite to conventional current, therefore electrons move from Y to X through R.
State the charge-rate equation. Current $I = Q/t$, so in time $t$ the charge passed is $Q = It$.
Relate charge to electron number. With $Q = N e$, the number per second is $N/t = I/e$.

Substitute values with units. $I = 3.2 \text{ mA} = 3.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}$ and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so $N/t = (3.2 \times 10^{-3})/(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ s}^{-1}$.
Combine direction and rate. Y to X with $2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ s}^{-1}$. This is option C.

options.A: The number $2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ s}^{-1}$ is correct for electrons per second, but X to Y is the conventional current direction, electrons move opposite to conventional current.
options.B: X to Y is the conventional current direction, not the electron direction, and $5.1 \times 10^{-22}$ is found by multiplying $I$ by $e$ instead of dividing by $e$.
options.C: Electrons move opposite to the $3.2 \text{ mA}$ conventional current, so Y to X, with rate $I/e = 2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ s}^{-1}$.
options.D: Y to X is the correct electron direction, but $5.1 \times 10^{-22} \text{ s}^{-1}$ is far too small and comes from calculating $I \times e$ instead of $I/e$.
